title: Engage in sustained oral communication and evaluate spoken texts

lessons.title: Taking part in discussions and meetings
lessons.html:
Speaking with purpose

A supervisor on a farm or in a plant talks all day: giving instructions at the morning line-up, running a toolbox talk on safety, discussing a problem with the farm manager, negotiating with a supplier or helping two workers settle a disagreement. Sustained oral communication means keeping a conversation or discussion going in a way that reaches its purpose.

Know your purpose and audience

Before you speak, ask yourself: why am I speaking (to inform, to instruct, to persuade, to solve a problem)? Who is listening (general workers, managers, a buyer, a government inspector)? What do they already know? What language are they most comfortable in? On many South African farms a team speaks several languages, so short sentences, plain words and checking understanding are essential. Use an interpreter you trust when needed.

Good discussion behaviour

  • Prepare: know the facts, figures and the decision that is needed.
  • Take turns. Do not interrupt; signal politely when you want to speak.
  • Ask open questions (what, how, why) to bring out ideas, and closed questions (yes or no) to confirm facts.
  • Support your points with reasons and examples: ‘We lost 40 crates of tomatoes last week because the cold room door was left open.’
  • Disagree with the idea, not the person. Say ‘I see it differently because…’ rather than ‘You are wrong.’
  • Summarise from time to time so everyone knows where the discussion stands.

Chairing a short meeting

  1. State the purpose and the time available.
  2. Go through the agenda items one by one.
  3. Give everyone a chance to speak, including quiet members.
  4. Keep the discussion on the topic and park side issues for later.
  5. End with clear decisions: who does what by when. Record these in minutes or a simple action list.

Body language and tone

Your tone of voice, facial expression, eye contact and posture send messages too. Crossed arms and a raised voice can make people defensive even when the words are correct. Remember that cultural norms differ: in some cultures avoiding direct eye contact with an older person is a sign of respect, not dishonesty. Stay calm, especially in conflict, and give people time to respond.

lessons.title: Planning and giving an oral presentation
lessons.html:
Presentations that people remember

You may have to present the month's production figures to management, explain a new procedure to a team, or report on a training course to colleagues. A clear structure is the key.

Structure

  • Introduction: greet, say who you are, state the topic and why it matters to the listeners. ‘Today I will show why our seed germination results dropped in March and what we propose to do.’
  • Body: two to four main points in a logical order, each supported by facts, examples or figures.
  • Conclusion: summarise the main points and state clearly what you want the audience to do or decide.

Using visual aids

A flip chart, handout, photograph or a few simple slides can help, especially with numbers. Keep each visual simple: one idea, large text, a clear graph. Do not read your slides aloud word for word; talk to the people. In the field, a real object works well, for example showing a damaged belt guard or an example of correctly labelled seed.

Delivery

  1. Practise beforehand and time yourself.
  2. Speak clearly and a little slower than in normal conversation.
  3. Vary your voice; a flat voice loses attention.
  4. Look at different people in the group.
  5. Use short notes or cue cards rather than a full script.
  6. Pause after an important point to let it sink in.

Handling questions

Invite questions at the end, or during the talk if the group is small. Listen to the whole question, repeat or rephrase it so everyone hears it, and answer briefly. If you do not know, say so and promise to find out by a certain time, then keep that promise. Never make up an answer, especially about safety, chemicals or animal health.

Adapting to the audience

The same information is presented differently to different listeners. To management you might focus on cost in rand and the decision needed; to a field team you focus on what changes in their work tomorrow and why it keeps them safe.

lessons.title: Listening critically and evaluating spoken texts
lessons.html:
Active and critical listening

Spoken texts include speeches, radio and podcast programmes, sales presentations, union and management addresses, farmers' day talks and conversations. Listening well means both understanding and judging what you hear.

Active listening

  • Give your full attention; put the phone away.
  • Show you are listening through nods and short responses.
  • Ask questions to clarify: ‘Do you mean every bay, or only the cold rooms?’
  • Paraphrase: ‘So you are saying the new pump will cut diesel use by about a quarter?’
  • Take short notes of key facts and actions.

Evaluating what you hear

Ask these questions about any spoken text:

  1. Purpose: is the speaker informing, persuading, selling or entertaining?
  2. Fact or opinion: can the statement be checked? ‘This product increased yields by 15% in our trials at three sites’ can be checked; ‘This is the best product on the market’ is opinion.
  3. Evidence: are figures, sources and examples given? Are they recent and relevant to your area?
  4. Bias: does the speaker gain from your agreement? A sales rep, a politician and an independent researcher may describe the same facts very differently.
  5. Techniques: watch for emotional appeals, exaggeration, repetition, flattery, and pressure such as ‘this price is only valid today’.
  6. What is left out: costs, risks or side effects that are not mentioned.

Language and tone

Notice word choice. Calling a change ‘restructuring’ or ‘retrenchments’ creates very different feelings. Notice tone, pace and register: is the language formal, informal, technical or full of jargon? Respectful language matters; discriminatory or insulting language is never acceptable in the workplace.

Responding

After evaluating a spoken text, respond in a balanced way: summarise what was said, state what you agree with and why, and raise questions or concerns supported by evidence.

Key points

  • Know your purpose and audience before you speak.
  • In discussions, take turns, ask questions, give reasons and summarise.
  • Structure presentations with an introduction, a few main points and a clear conclusion.
  • Listen actively: attend, clarify, paraphrase and note.
  • Evaluate spoken texts for purpose, fact versus opinion, evidence, bias and persuasive techniques.

quiz.question: What should you do if you are asked a question you cannot answer during a presentation?

options.text: Give your best guess as if it were a fact
Ignore the question
End the presentation
Say you do not know and promise to find out by a set time

This is the best product on the market
Yield increased by 15% in the trial
The trial was done in 2025

Please speak louder.
